key_insight: Machine-learned simulations show that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far more slowly than in the bulk because surface geometry removes efficient hopping pathways.
engineering_relevance: This helps explain the low electron mobility in porous rutile TiO2 and informs the design of oxide surfaces for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to a redox-active oxide surface
Ran several nanoseconds of finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110)
Analyzed polaron hopping pathways, layer-resolved mobility, and vacancy-induced free-energy changes
evidence_signal: The study uses nanosecond-scale simulations across a temperature range and reports several-orders-of-magnitude lower surface mobility than in the corresponding bulk material.
watch_item: The conclusions depend on the accuracy and transferability of the machine-learned model for capturing rare hopping events and vacancy effects on complex surfaces.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
